summary.text: Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of a crystalline compound forms from its separated gaseous constituents.
It measures the cohesive forces that bind crystalline solids and is linked to properties such as solubility, hardness and volatility.
It generally cannot be measured directly, so it is usually deduced from experimental data using the Born-Haber cycle.

items.prompt: Two ionic crystals have ions of nearly the same size, but one has ions with double the charge. Which has the stronger lattice energy?

options.label: The one with doubly charged ions
The one with singly charged ions
They match, since the sizes are similar
Neither, as charge has no effect on lattice energy

items.explain: Lattice energy depends strongly on ion charges, and the difference in charge numbers is the principal reason BaO's is so much larger than NaCl's despite similar bond radii.

options.label: Read it straight off a thermometer
Deduce it from experimental data using a Born-Haber cycle

items.prompt: Two ions of the same charge are packed with different spacing. Which crystal has the lower lattice energy?

options.label: The one with ions closer together
The one whose ions are mostly neutral
The one with ions farther apart
Neither, as spacing has no effect

items.explain: Large values of the ion distance r₀ result in low lattice energies, whereas high ionic charges give high lattice energies.

items.prompt: One textbook lists the lattice energy of NaCl as -786 kJ/mol and another as +786. How can both be right?

options.label: One of the books measured a different compound
The crystal changes sign when it is heated
The two books use opposite sign conventions
Lattice energy has no fixed size

items.explain: Some books define lattice energy as the energy required to separate the crystal into ions, with the opposite sign, and both conventions are widely used.

items.prompt: Forming a lattice from separate ions drops the internal energy. What explains this?

options.label: The net attractive forces between the ions
The loss of all charge on the ions
The increase in volume as the solid forms
The melting of the gaseous ions into a liquid

items.explain: Forming a crystal lattice from ions in vacuum lowers the internal energy because of the net attractive forces involved.

items.prompt: When is the Kapustinskii equation a sensible choice?

options.label: When the exact lattice energy of a pure ion must be found to many digits
When only compounds without any charge are involved
When a quick estimate is wanted and high precision is not required
When the crystal has been heated above its melting point

items.explain: It is an approximation that makes calculations easier than the Born-Lande equation, suited to quick estimates where high precision is not required.

paragraphs.heading: What lattice energy is
paragraphs.text: Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of a crystalline compound forms from its parts. The starting point is imagined as those parts spread infinitely far apart, as a gas, at 0 K (−273.15 °C). In effect, it measures the cohesive forces that hold a crystalline solid together.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The size of the lattice energy is tied to many other physical properties of a solid, including its solubility, hardness and volatility. In general it cannot be measured directly. Instead it is usually worked out from experimental data, using a method called the Born–Haber cycle.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to write the sign
paragraphs.text: When a crystal forms from ions in a vacuum, the net attraction between them must lower the internal energy, so on this view the lattice energy is negative. Some textbooks, and the widely used CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, flip the sign. They define it as the energy needed to break the crystal apart into separated gaseous ions, a process that takes in energy. By that convention the lattice energy of NaCl is +786 kJ/mol, and both conventions are in wide use.

paragraphs.heading: Charge and size
paragraphs.text: The lattice energy of an ionic compound depends strongly on the charges of its ions, which attract or repel each other according to Coulomb's law. The sizes of the ions matter too, in a subtler way. A larger distance to the closest ion gives a lower lattice energy, while higher ionic charges give a higher one. London dispersion forces between the ions also contribute, through polarization effects.

paragraphs.heading: Equations to estimate it
paragraphs.text: In 1918 Max Born and Alfred Landé proposed working it out from the electric potential of the ionic lattice plus a repulsive term. Their equation combines electrostatic interactions with a repulsion that follows a power law, set by a number called the Born exponent, n. In 1956 Anatolii Kapustinskii developed a general empirical equation that works for many kinds of ionic compound, complex ions included. It is simpler to use than the Born–Landé equation and suits quick estimates where high precision is not needed.

paragraphs.heading: Barium oxide versus sodium chloride
paragraphs.text: Barium oxide (BaO) has the same crystal structure as sodium chloride (NaCl), and their bond radii are close: 275 picometers against 283. Yet the lattice energy of BaO is −3054 kJ/mol, while that of NaCl is only −786 kJ/mol. The difference lies in the charges, since BaO's ions carry +2 and −2 and NaCl's carry +1 and −1. The Born–Landé equation points to these charges as the main reason for the large gap.

paragraphs.heading: When polarization counts
paragraphs.text: For some ionic compounds, polarization effects have to be included in the calculation explicitly. Iron pyrite, FeS₂, is one example. Leaving polarization out produced a 15% difference between theory and experiment for FeS₂, while including it brought the error down to 2%.
